newsitem.title: GERMANY: FDP tax cut drive angers German coalition allies.
newsitem.headline: FDP tax cut drive angers German coalition allies.

text.p: Germany's Free Democrats (FDP), increasingly a loose cannon in Chancellor Helmut Kohl's ruling alliance, strained coalition ties on Monday by demanding the abolition by 2000 of a tax levied to rebuild eastern Germany.

At their traditional conference at Epiphany -- the day the three kings brought gifts for the infant Jesus -- FDP chiefs pressed for tax giveaways in the hope of winning enough votes to survive as a national force at general elections next year.

Party leader Wolfgang Gerhardt told delegates in the southern city of Stuttgart that scrapping the so-called solidarity surcharge "has become a symbol of whether the state will cut the tax burden on citizens and businesses".

Opinion polls show that the FDP is dangerously close to the minimum five percent of votes required to guarantee reelection to parliament. Under the threat, it has turned to the single issue of tax cuts for electoral salvation.

But calls for the solidarity surcharge's abolition have angered the powerful Christian Democrat parties (CDU/CSU) in Kohl's 14-year-old coalition. The FDP demand comes after a row was settled before Christmas by agreeing a two-point cut in the tax to 5.5 percent in 1998.
Finance Minister Theo Waigel, leader of the Bavarian CSU, said abolishing the solidarity tax would double the amount of spending cuts needed under a tax reform planned for 1999.

"The FDP is making it all look too easy when it demands the abolition of the solidarity charge at a given moment, without saying a word on how it will be financed," he told the Neue Passauer Zeitung in an interview to be published on Tuesday.
Kohl's CDU has already repudiated the FDP demand in the bluntest terms, saying anyone seeking the surcharge's abolition had no right to be taken seriously.

The renewed tax row comes just as a coalition working group is finalising the tax reforms, intended to make big income tax cuts while ensuring Germany can still stick to the borrowing limits required under European monetary union.
The commission's work is already behind schedule. The reopening of the coalition's war of words means it might miss its target of finalising its tax strategy this month.
German President Roman Herzog has made a rare intervention in the day-to-day political debate to express his exasperation at the almost non-stop coalition debate on the solidarity tax.
And the opposition Social Democrats (SPD) said the row was turning the issue into a political football being kicked around by coalition bigwigs in Bonn.

"A decision on when and how the solidarity tax should be reduced should be linked to concrete progress in rebuilding east Germany," Manfred Stolpe, SPD premier of the eastern state of Brandenburg, told Monday's Handelsblatt newspaper.

None of the criticism looks likely to deter the FDP from its line. The party has few votes to lose in the east, while the CDU faces grassroots pressure to prolong costly job schemes which have capped regional unemployment at a high 15 percent.

At their congress, the FDP leaders also called for reform of the education and pensions systems, cuts in state spending -- now over 50 percent of gross domestic product -- and changes to Germany's pay bargaining system.

But the party still sees tax cutting as its top priority. Talking to Monday's mass-circulation Bild newspaper, Economics Minister Guenter Rexrodt, also a member of the FDP, linked the solidarity tax issue to the whole tax reform debate.
"There is no point trying to stimulate the economy with a major tax reform while retaining the solidarity tax," Rexrodt said. "The solidarity tax must go by the year 2000."
